title: Management of vernal keratoconjunctivitis: Navigating a changing treatment landscape
clinical_background: VKC is a chronic, progressive ocular inflammatory disorder that can threaten vision and primarily affects children and young adults. Its prevalence varies substantially across regions. Because it is uncommon in some settings and resembles other forms of allergic conjunctivitis, diagnosis and treatment may be delayed until symptoms substantially impair quality of life. Although VKC was previously considered mainly an IgE-mediated condition, approximately 50% of patients show no allergic sensitization. Multiple inflammatory pathways contribute to its ocular manifestations and characteristic conjunctival lesions.
objectives: Review how understanding of the immunopathology of VKC has evolved.
Describe the expanding range of treatments for VKC.
Examine the clinical implications of emerging treatment approaches.
Discuss future directions for VKC research and clinical practice.
study_design: Narrative review based on a PubMed Medline search covering 2016 through 2022. The authors prioritized prospective studies and randomized clinical trials, considered other relevant study types, and checked reference lists for additional articles.

population.description: People with vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC); no single patient cohort was enrolled for this review.
inclusion_criteria: Relevant English-language articles addressing VKC diagnosis, treatment, prevalence, presentation, signs, symptoms, incidence, or pathogenesis.
Relevant articles identified through the reference lists of selected publications.

interpretation: VKC is a progressive ocular surface disease that can threaten vision and substantially impair quality of life. Its resemblance to other allergic conjunctivitides, particularly where VKC is uncommon, can delay diagnosis and treatment. The authors describe VKC as involving IgE-dependent and other immune pathways, which helps explain why treatments directed only at histamine or mast cells may not adequately control it. CsA CE 0.1% provides an approved corticosteroid-sparing option, while other topical and systemic approaches remain under investigation. Treatment needs to reflect disease severity, corneal involvement and individual patient needs.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors contrast the earlier view of VKC as predominantly IgE-mediated with evidence of additional cellular and inflammatory pathways; approximately 50% of patients do not show allergic sensitization. They note that meta-analyses of topical treatments have generally not established significant efficacy differences among commonly used agents. A 2007 meta-analysis of 27 double-masked trials involving 1092 patients found improvement in VKC signs and symptoms with every evaluated drug. A later review of 45 articles involving 1749 patients and 20 drugs likewise found improvement across treatments without significant differences between individual drugs. Comparative studies of tacrolimus and compounded cyclosporine have produced mixed findings, and the authors report no direct comparison of tacrolimus with CsA CE 0.1%.
clinical_implications: Delayed recognition and treatment of VKC may allow vision-threatening corneal complications and greater impairment of daily functioning and quality of life.
Because allergic sensitization is absent in approximately 50% of patients with VKC, allergen-specific immunotherapy is applicable to a relatively limited group.
Topical mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines and NSAIDs can relieve symptoms but have little or no effect on the broader immune processes underlying VKC.
Corticosteroids can control active ocular inflammation, but their potentially serious ocular adverse effects constrain prolonged use; CsA CE 0.1% offers a corticosteroid-sparing alternative.
Responses can differ across individual signs and symptoms, so a composite efficacy score may obscure clinically relevant treatment effects.
practice_implications: Recognize VKC promptly and align treatment with severity, underlying pathology, corneal involvement, symptom pattern and the patient's needs and goals.
Consider VKC when treatment for allergic conjunctivitis does not resolve symptoms; the article states that a definitive diagnosis requires limbal and/or tarsal papillae.
Identify relevant allergens and irritants and reduce exposure. Wraparound sunglasses, visored caps, artificial tears and cold compresses are described as supportive measures.
Educate patients and caregivers about VKC's chronic course and treatment options, teach eye-drop instillation, address psychosocial barriers and support adherence.

Avoid indiscriminate topical corticosteroid use. The cited EAACI position paper advises against making these agents the first treatment choice for ocular allergy and recommends ophthalmologist monitoring during their use. The article favors an acute pulse of 3–4 drops per day for 5 days; longer courses should be limited to 1–3 weeks and tapered over several days.

For active VKC unresponsive to nonsteroidal treatment, low-potency corticosteroids are usually prescribed before high-potency agents; the latter are recommended only if low-potency treatment does not achieve the intended clinical effect.

The cited EAACI position paper recommends CsA eye drops to spare corticosteroid use in corticosteroid-dependent VKC and reserves off-label tacrolimus eye drops or ointment for severe VKC refractory to CsA.
Consider allergen-specific immunotherapy when reactions to specific allergens are established, while recognizing its limited applicability across all patients with VKC.
Account for the impact of VKC on quality of life and incorporate validated measures such as the QUICK questionnaire into treatment plans.
limitations: Much of the available VKC research consists of small, nonrandomized studies, limiting the ability to detect potentially important differences between treatments.
Variation in study designs, populations, outcomes, formulations and dosing schedules makes comparisons difficult and limits conclusions for treatment selection in routine care.

The authors describe tacrolimus evidence as relying substantially on case reports, case series and small uncontrolled studies with differing regimens; comparative findings against compounded cyclosporine are mixed.
A lack of standardized diagnostic criteria and differences in regional diagnosis, clinical practice and access to care complicate both VKC recognition and reliable prevalence estimates.
Composite outcome scores may conceal differing effects on individual VKC signs and symptoms.
open_questions: How do available VKC therapies compare when efficacy and safety are assessed in adequately powered studies?
What sequence or combination of therapies is optimal, and could allergen-specific immunotherapy act synergistically with topical treatments?
Which diagnostic criteria and core treatment outcomes should be adopted consistently for VKC?
How does climate-related geographic variation compare across regions, and what contribution do genetic factors make to VKC development?
What effect do supratarsal corticosteroid injections have on intraocular pressure? The cited studies report differing findings.
How do tacrolimus and CsA CE 0.1% compare directly in patients with VKC?
future_directions: Conduct adequately powered comparative studies of VKC treatments to strengthen the evidence supporting diagnostic criteria and treatment guidance.
Determine effective treatment sequences and combinations, including possible interactions between immunotherapy and topical agents.
Reach consensus on core VKC outcomes and report results separately for individual signs and symptoms to support more individualized treatment.
Include validated quality-of-life assessments, such as the QUICK questionnaire, in future trials and clinical planning.
Collect comparative epidemiological data across different climates and clarify the role of genetic factors in VKC.

main_conclusion: VKC requires timely recognition because diagnostic delays in this progressive disorder can impair vision, daily functioning and quality of life. Its multiple immune pathways support individualized management; approval of CsA CE 0.1% provides a corticosteroid-sparing option, while additional targeted treatments remain under investigation. The authors emphasize education, avoidance of relevant triggers and support for adherence alongside treatment tailored to each patient.
narrative_summary:
This narrative review examined VKC epidemiology, clinical presentation, immunopathology and treatment using a PubMed Medline search covering 2016 through 2022, supplemented by reference lists. VKC principally affects younger people but can persist or arise in adults. Its resemblance to other allergic conjunctivitides can delay diagnosis; limbal and/or tarsal papillae are required for a definitive diagnosis, and inadequately treated disease can threaten vision. Approximately 50% of patients lack allergic sensitization, consistent with immune activity extending beyond IgE to Th2 cells, eosinophils and inflammatory mediators.

The authors describe trigger avoidance and supportive measures alongside therapies selected according to severity, corneal involvement and patient needs. Mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines and NSAIDs can relieve symptoms, whereas corticosteroids offer strong anti-inflammatory effects but carry potentially serious ocular risks that constrain prolonged use. Calcineurin inhibitors are corticosteroid-sparing options. In the cited VEKTIS trial, CsA CE 0.1% given q.i.d. or b.i.d. improved the composite efficacy score versus vehicle at 4 months (P = 0.007 and P = 0.010, respectively); rescue medication was required by 32.1% of the q.i.d. group versus 53.4% of the vehicle group (P = 0.010). Evidence for other emerging approaches remains varied. Small, heterogeneous studies limit comparisons between treatments. The authors call for adequately powered comparative research, separate reporting of clinical outcomes and greater attention to validated quality-of-life measures.

notable_adverse_events: Topical mast cell stabilizers: transient stinging or burning on instillation was described as the most common side effect.
Topical antihistamines: transient burning and a dry sensation were listed as class-associated effects.
Dual-acting agents: transient burning was listed; benzalkonium chloride in most formulations may cause ocular surface toxicity.

Topical NSAIDs: burning/stinging occurred more often than with placebo in a cited allergic-conjunctivitis meta-analysis. Prolonged use can cause corneal toxicity, and use may increase the risk of corneal melt.
Topical corticosteroids: reported risks include increased intraocular pressure, onset or worsening of glaucoma, cataracts, delayed wound healing, and increased risk of viral or fungal superinfection.

Corticosteroid-induced glaucoma in children with VKC: reported rates ranged from 2% in Italy to 19% in India. In the Indian study, 36% of children presented with visual impairment from corticosteroid-induced glaucoma that met World Health Organization criteria for blindness.
Topical difluprednate: clinically significant intraocular-pressure increases were significantly more likely in children than in adults.
Supratarsal corticosteroids: reports differed on intraocular pressure; some found no increase, whereas others reported increases in 6% to 17% of treated patients.

Compounded cyclosporine: ocular opportunistic infection risk, burning, and irritation were reported. Earlier 2% formulations were associated with treatment-limiting transient burning and foreign body sensation on instillation.

CsA CE pooled NOVATIVE and VEKTIS analysis: instillation-site pain was reported in 9.4% of high-dose and 7.5% of low-dose recipients; pruritis was reported in 5.2% of high-dose and 7.5% of low-dose recipients. Most adverse events were mild-to-moderate, and systemic CsA absorption was negligible with both regimens.

Topical tacrolimus: ocular burning on instillation and increased risk of corneal infections were reported. In a 24-patient comparison with CsA 2%, tacrolimus caused slightly less bothersome burning on instillation, with no significant between-group safety difference; in a separate 30-child crossover trial, side effects were generally mild and similar for tacrolimus and cyclosporine, and serum levels of both drugs were negligible.
Montelukast: the treatment table reported no adverse events for the cited study.

Dupilumab: conjunctivitis and keratitis were more frequent among recipients in clinical trials; a claims analysis of N = 2144 also found more encounters for ocular surface disorders after treatment began. The treatment table reported no adverse events for the cited VKC report.
Rebamipide: dysgeusia and eyelid pruritus were reported.
Omalizumab: the treatment table reported no adverse events for the cited report.

secondary_results: VEKTIS identified CFS score as a secondary endpoint; change from baseline in CFS was the principal contributor to the composite efficacy-score improvement, accounting for 70.3% of the treatment effect with CsA CE 0.1% q.i.d. and 77.6% with CsA CE 0.1% b.i.d.

VEKTIS reported significant improvements versus vehicle with CsA CE 0.1% q.i.d. in photophobia (P < 0.001), tearing (P < 0.009), itching (P = 0.001), mucous discharge (P = 0.005), and quality of life (P < 0.05).

During the VEKTIS 4-month efficacy period, 32.1% of the CsA CE 0.1% q.i.d. group versus 53.4% of the vehicle group required 1 or more courses of rescue medication (P = 0.010); the reported improvements in keratitis, symptoms, and quality of life persisted through the 8-month extension.

document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a persistent, progressive ocular inflammatory disease that can threaten vision and mainly affects children and young adults. Its prevalence ranges from <2 per 10,000 in the United States to as high as 1,100 per 10,000 in parts of Africa. Where VKC is uncommon, distinguishing it from other conditions can be difficult; treatment may begin only after disease progression and substantial impairment of quality of life. Although VKC was formerly regarded chiefly as an immunoglobulin E-mediated disorder, approximately 50% of affected patients lack allergic sensitization. Multiple inflammatory pathways contribute to its manifestations and characteristic conjunctival eosinophilic and fibroproliferative lesions. This review examines changes in understanding of VKC immunopathology, available and emerging treatments, their clinical implications, and priorities for research and practice.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: VKC is a persistent and progressive inflammatory eye disorder with potential to impair vision. It mainly occurs in children and adolescents (<20 years), and onset precedes 10 years of age in most cases. Although it commonly subsides at puberty, prospective and retrospective analyses indicate that up to 12% of patients with VKC are adults and that up to 82% of adult cases begin after puberty. Similarities to other allergic conjunctivitides contribute to diagnostic errors and delayed treatment. Advances in understanding VKC immunopathology have prompted additional therapeutic options. The review addresses the changing treatment landscape, implications of emerging approaches, and future research and practice.

document_sections.heading: 2. Epidemiology of VKC
document_sections.content: VKC represents less than 1% of ocular diseases in developed countries, but prevalence differs considerably across regions. It occurs most often in warm, dry, windy settings with abundant environmental allergens, including central Africa, Japan, India, and South America; reports also come from North America, China, Australia, Great Britain, and Sweden. A community-based cross-sectional study of 574 children in southwest Ethiopia reported 11.1% prevalence, with male sex, close animal contact, dust exposure, and systemic allergy history associated with greater risk. A cross-sectional study in northwest Ethiopia (N = 737) reported 5.8% prevalence and identified kerosene/firewood cooking, dust exposure, and previous nonocular allergic disease as risk factors. A nested population-based case-control study in randomly chosen Rwandan primary schools (N = 3,041) reported 4.0% prevalence; hot, dry climate, male sex, and higher economic status were associated with increased risk. A cross-sectional survey sent to 3,003 ophthalmologists in Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden yielded national prevalence estimates ranging from 1.16 to 10.55 per 10,000. A United States healthcare-claims analysis estimated 1.24 per 10,000 people among individuals <18 years of age. Proposed explanations for geographic variation include population genetics, migration, age composition, climate, socioeconomic circumstances, and interactions among lifestyle, genes, and environment. Differences in diagnostic criteria, practice, and healthcare access, together with limited awareness among patients, caregivers, and clinicians, hinder accurate prevalence estimation. Comparative epidemiological research across climates is needed to clarify prevalence and genetic contributions.

document_sections.heading: 3. Signs and symptoms
document_sections.content: VKC produces papillary changes in the upper tarsal conjunctiva and around the limbus. The distribution defines 3 subtypes: tarsal, limbal, and mixed. Tarsal VKC features cobblestone-like upper tarsal papillae measuring >1.0 mm in diameter. Limbal VKC commonly features Horner-Trantas dots, reflecting limbal conjunctival infiltration and inflammatory-mediator release by eosinophils, mast cells, and lymphocytes. Mixed VKC involves both sites. Manifestations include ocular redness, itching, foreign-body sensation, tearing, mucous discharge, thickened eyelids, and associated pseudoptosis; corneal disease can also cause pain. Although manifestations overlap with allergic conjunctivitis, marked photophobia and ocular pain are more specific to VKC. Persistent symptoms despite topical and/or systemic antihistamines used for allergic conjunctivitis should raise suspicion; confirmation requires limbal and/or tarsal papillae. Inadequately treated disease can produce corneal neovascularization or shield ulcers, while subsequent reepithelialization can lead to astigmatism, keratoconus, amblyopia, or corneal perforation. Table 1 compares clinical features of ocular allergic conditions. Several severity schemes are described. The Bonini system in Table 2 is widely used. Gokhale and colleagues proposed a system incorporating ocular findings, symptoms, and chronicity, with 5 categories: mild, moderate intermittent, moderate chronic, severe, and blinding; findings considered include Horner-Trantas dots, cobblestone papillae, superficial punctate keratitis, and macro-erosions. A fluorescein-staining approach associated with the VKC-Collaborative Longitudinal Evaluation of Keratoconus study (CLEK) divides the cornea and limbus into 5 regions: central, superior, nasal, inferior, and temporal limbal. Regional scores are summed, using 0–4 centrally and 0–1 for each limbal area; totals <3 indicate mild disease, >3 to <6 moderate disease, and >6 severe disease.

document_sections.heading: 4. Pathogenesis
document_sections.content: VKC was previously characterized as an immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated disease. The immediate type 1 IgE-mediated response induces IgE antibody production and acute itching, swelling, and inflammation. IgE binding activates mast cells, releasing histamine; interferon (IFN); interleukin (IL)-4, -5, and -13; tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α); CCL5, CCL11, and CCL17; tryptase; prostaglandins; and leukotrienes. Leukotrienes have been detected in tears from patients with allergic conjunctivitis, including VKC. Nevertheless, approximately 50% of patients with VKC have no allergic sensitization despite involvement of allergic-conjunctivitis immune pathways. In a Florence case series of 110 patients with VKC (mean age, 8.3 years), 69% had no other allergies and 45% had IgE sensitization. In a retrospective Italian study of 195 children (mean age at symptom onset, 7.1 years), 59% had no other allergic conditions and 50% had negative skin tests without evidence of IgE sensitization. These observations may help explain why topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers usually do not adequately control VKC; sensitization status may also distinguish phenotypes. Beyond IgE responses, VKC involves a T-cell-mediated, lymphocyte T-helper (Th2) type 2-driven late allergic response, with eosinophil infiltration and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Activated conjunctival CD4+ Th2 lymphocytes and other immune cells release IL-4, IL-13, and TNF-α. These mediators activate corneal fibroblasts, promoting excessive extracellular-matrix deposition and conjunctival fibroproliferative lesions. Cytokines also activate eosinophils, whose proteins and matrix metalloproteinases damage corneal epithelium, facilitate further cytokine access to fibroblasts, and intensify inflammation. Conjunctival biopsies show eosinophil infiltration; elevated tear eosinophil cationic protein and major basic protein have been linked to epithelial injury and disease severity. Conjunctival infiltrates in VKC also contain CD4+ lymphocytes, mast cells, basophils, dendritic cells, and macrophages.

document_sections.heading: 5. Diagnostic challenges and impact
document_sections.content: Because VKC is relatively uncommon, particularly in developed countries, eye-care professionals may miss or recognize it late, postponing treatment until advanced stages. Early episodes can be brief and intermittent, escape notice, or be mistaken for allergic conjunctivitis. A small United Kingdom study found intervals of 0 to 6 years between initial symptoms and VKC diagnosis. Progression and treatment delays can culminate in infectious keratitis, shield ulcers, corneal scars, corneal perforation, keratoconus, irregular astigmatism, and amblyopia. Symptom overlap with other conjunctivitides and the absence of standardized diagnostic criteria complicate care. In practice, assessment of clinical features and severity scales such as the Bonini grading system usually guide diagnosis and management. VKC markedly affects quality of life (QoL), including the ability to participate in outdoor activities or activities that increase allergen exposure. In a prospective observational case series, 30 children with active VKC (mean age, 9.5 ± 2.1 years) identified symptoms and activity restrictions that informed the validated 16-item Quality of Life in Children with Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (QUICK) questionnaire. In that series, VKC interfered with meeting friends for 58%, swimming in a pool for 71%, sports for 58%, and outdoor play for 40%. An Egyptian cross-sectional study of schoolchildren with VKC (N = 126) reported missed school days in 30%, impaired concentration in 41%, homework difficulties in 40%, and difficulty attending school in 47%. A Rwandan school-age case-control study (N = 121) found that children with VKC were 3–5 times more likely than unaffected children to miss school for an ocular reason. A qualitative study involving 9 children and their families identified repeated daily eye-drop administration, especially at school, as difficult; school personnel were sometimes unwilling to administer drops. A prospective Chinese case-control study found significantly poorer QoL and greater worry among parents of children with VKC (n = 23)/atopic keratoconjunctivitis (n = 7) than among parents of children without allergic conjunctivitis (n = 96) or with seasonal/perennial allergic conjunctivitis (n = 62).

document_sections.heading: 6. Treatment approaches
document_sections.content: Timely recognition and treatment are important for reducing vision-threatening consequences. Treatment aims to relieve acute symptoms, prevent recurrence, limit treatment-related harm, and improve QoL. Ideally, choices reflect each patient's clinical status. Because exacerbations often arise in spring and summer, some experts recommend beginning therapy then and continuing it throughout the year when needed.

document_sections.heading: 6.1. Nonpharmacologic measures
document_sections.content: Identifying allergens or irritants and limiting exposure are central to VKC care. Wraparound sunglasses and visor caps may reduce exposure to environmental triggers such as dust and sunlight. Artificial tears can wash and dilute allergens, inflammatory mediators, and cells in the tear film. Cold compresses during exacerbations may temporarily ease sensory symptoms, swelling, and redness. Table 3 summarizes established and emerging treatments. Chronic VKC and prolonged treatment impose demands on patients, caregivers, and clinicians. School-age children and their caregivers may find behavioral changes and complicated regimens particularly difficult to sustain. Education about disease course and chronicity, instruction in correct drop instillation, and help with psychosocial burdens support adherence and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 6.2. Pharmacologic measures
document_sections.content: Recognition of distinct VKC phenotypes and their complex immune mechanisms has stimulated investigation of therapies aimed more directly at inflammatory processes responsible for proliferative changes and corneal injury. Available options include approved and off-label treatments with differing efficacy across disease manifestations and severity.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1. Symptomatic treatment
document_sections.content: Topical mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs) can relieve VKC symptoms, but have little or no effect on the underlying complex immune response.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.1. Topical mast cell stabilizers ± antihistamines.
document_sections.content: Mast cell stabilizers inhibit mast cell activation and degranulation, reducing mediator release and influx of eosinophils, neutrophils, and monocytes. Often used early in VKC treatment, they include cromolyn sodium 2% and 4%, nedocromil sodium 2%, N-acetyl-aspartyl-glutamate (NAAGA) 6%, and lodoxamide 0.1%. In a randomized, double-masked trial involving children and adults with VKC (N = 65), topical cromolyn sodium 4% relieved signs and symptoms significantly better than placebo. Nedocromil sodium acts on eosinophils, neutrophils, mast cells, macrophages, monocytes, and platelets. A study in children with VKC (N = 36) found that nedocromil sodium 2% acted sooner than cromolyn sodium 2%, with significantly greater improvement in itching, grittiness, redness, and keratitis within 6 weeks, and significantly greater reductions in redness, keratitis, papillae, and pannus at 22 weeks. Another comparison of nedocromil sodium 2%, cromolyn sodium 2%, and placebo in 138 children and adults found significantly greater reductions in disease severity with either active drug than placebo, and a stronger symptom effect with nedocromil sodium than cromolyn sodium. NAAGA also reduces effects of complement activation, leukotriene production, and expression of eosinophil adhesion molecules. In a randomized pilot comparison of NAAGA and levocabastine eye drops (N = 23), tear eosinophil cationic protein fell significantly more with NAAGA; a similar pattern for change from baseline in total ocular symptom score was not statistically significant. Lodoxamide reduces eosinophil activation and degranulation and has been shown to significantly lower tear tryptase and eosinophil levels. A single-arm VKC study (N = 40) found significant improvement in signs and symptoms, with 38 of 40 patients symptom-free at study end. A comparative study of 30 patients found lodoxamide ophthalmic solution 0.1% significantly better than cromolyn sodium ophthalmic solution 4% for reducing CD4+ and CD23+ cell numbers and clinical manifestations. In another study of 95 patients, lodoxamide 0.1% ophthalmic solution improved physician- and patient-assessed outcomes more than levocabastine 0.05% ophthalmic suspension. Both improved symptoms significantly from baseline, but lodoxamide produced significantly greater improvement in conjunctival discharge, photophobia, tearing, itching, and bulbar conjunctiva at one or more time points. Transient stinging and burning are the most frequent adverse effects of mast cell stabilizers, and regimens can require up to 6 administrations daily. Antihistamines compete with histamine at histamine type 1 (H1) receptors. Topical H1 blockers are often combined with mast cell stabilizers to address itching and swelling. Selective newer H1 blockers such as levocabastine and emedastine are recommended in this setting because of better tolerability and longer action than older agents such as pheniramine and antazoline. Topical antihistamine relief begins rapidly but lasts relatively briefly, generally requiring up to 4 instillations daily. Dual-acting drugs provide immediate antihistamine activity and longer-lasting mast cell stabilization. Examples are olopatadine 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.7%; bepotastine besilate 1.5%; azelastine 0.05%; and alcaftadine 0.2%. Except for preservative-free unit doses, most contain benzalkonium chloride, which may harm the ocular surface. Olopatadine hydrochloride was the first such drug approved for chronic and seasonal allergic conjunctivitis in the United States and European Union. It inhibits anti-IgE-driven mast cell up-regulation of intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) on conjunctival epithelial cells; reported benefits include less itching, redness, and eyelid swelling and better QoL. In a prospective VKC study (N = 20), olopatadine hydrochloride 0.1% significantly improved signs and symptoms at 2 months and reduced goblet-cell density. Bepotastine besilate inhibits IL-5, leukotrienes, platelet-activating factor, and eosinophil migration and is effective against itching in allergic conjunctivitis. An open-label randomized VKC study (N = 50) found that olopatadine 0.1% and bepotastine besilate 1.5% both reduced signs and symptoms after 8 weeks; olopatadine significantly reduced papillary hypertrophy, whereas bepotastine besilate reduced ocular discomfort, watering, and capillary hyperemia. Azelastine combines rapid histamine blockade with sustained mast cell stabilization. In a prospective VKC study (N = 76), tacrolimus 0.1% alone and tacrolimus 0.1% plus azelastine 0.05% significantly improved Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) scores from baseline at every follow-up visit. The combination reduced OSDI more than monotherapy at 1 week and yielded significantly greater improvements in conjunctival redness, papillae, and corneal involvement. Alcaftadine 0.25% has been available without prescription in the United States since 2021 to prevent allergic-conjunctivitis-related ocular itching. A pooled analysis of two double-masked conjunctival allergen challenge trials among patients with ocular allergy histories (N = 284) found alcaftadine 0.25% significantly more effective than olopatadine 0.2% against challenge-induced itching 16 hours after dosing. In an allergic-conjunctivitis mouse model, alcaftadine inhibited eosinophil recruitment more than olopatadine, possibly by preserving epithelial junction protein markers.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.2. Topical NSAIDs.
document_sections.content: Topical NSAIDs discussed include ketorolac tromethamine (0.5%, 0.3%), approved for allergic conjunctivitis, and diclofenac sodium 0.1%. They suppress release of itch-associated prostaglandins E2 and I2. In a prospective VKC study of 21 patients, topical ketorolac reduced itching significantly more than placebo. Another prospective VKC study (N = 22) found sustained control of signs and symptoms with diclofenac sodium 0.1% drops. A 2007 meta-analysis of 8 placebo-controlled allergic-conjunctivitis studies (N = 712) supported NSAID efficacy against conjunctival itching and injection but found more burning or stinging. Extended topical use can damage the cornea, restricting usefulness when corneal involvement is present, and NSAIDs can increase the risk of corneal melt.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2.1. Topical corticosteroids.
document_sections.content: Corticosteroids act on early and late allergic responses and are described as the most effective anti-inflammatory agents for active ocular allergy, including VKC. Their usefulness in chronic disease is constrained by increased intraocular pressure, onset or worsening of glaucoma, cataracts, delayed healing, and greater risk of viral and fungal superinfection. Inappropriate prescribing and insufficient monitoring heighten concern: an Indian eye-center retrospective study found approximately 17% of presenting patients used topical corticosteroids without medical supervision, with a mean exposure of 21.3 months. The American Academy of Ophthalmology’s Preferred Practice Pattern cautions against indiscriminate topical corticosteroid use. The European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (EAACI) advises against using them as the initial choice for ocular allergy and recommends ophthalmologist monitoring during treatment. For acute ocular allergy, a pulse of 3–4 drops daily for 5 days is preferred; longer courses should be limited to 1–3 weeks and tapered gradually over several days. Corticosteroids suppress inflammatory-cell infiltration, mast cell proliferation, cellular immune responses, and production of prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and platelet-activating factor. Structure influences safety and efficacy. Ketone-containing ophthalmic corticosteroids at the C-20 position—including prednisolone phosphate 1%, dexamethasone sodium phosphate 0.1%, difluprednate 0.05%, betamethasone sodium 0.1%, fluorometholone acetate 0.1%, and rimexolone 1%—are thought to create corticosteroid-protein adducts potentially contributing to cataracts with extended treatment. Loteprednol 0.5% instead has a 17β-chloromethyl ester at the C-20 position, allowing rapid conversion to an inactive metabolite, less systemic absorption, and lower ocular adverse-effect risk than ketone corticosteroids. VKC corticosteroids are grouped as low potency (fluorometholone, loteprednol, rimexolone) or high potency (prednisolone, dexamethasone, difluprednate, betamethasone). In a comparison involving 57 patients with VKC, loteprednol etabonate 0.5% and prednisolone each improved signs and symptoms significantly more than fluorometholone, except for chemosis. Low-potency agents have relatively limited ocular penetration and are generally the first steroids used when active VKC does not respond to nonsteroidal treatment. High-potency agents provide greater anti-inflammatory effects but pose more adverse-effect risk, especially in children. Children receiving topical difluprednate have significantly greater risk than adults of clinically important intraocular-pressure increases. Pediatric VKC studies reported corticosteroid-induced glaucoma rates ranging from 2% in Italy to 19% in India. In the Indian study, 36% of children presented with visual impairment due to corticosteroid-induced glaucoma that fulfilled World Health Organization blindness criteria. High-potency corticosteroids are consequently recommended only if lower-potency agents do not achieve the desired effect. Case reports suggest that severe VKC resistant to topical and/or systemic corticosteroids, including palpebral disease with giant papillae, may improve after supratarsal corticosteroid injection. A single-center retrospective review reported symptom resolution and improved visual acuity after supratarsal triamcinolone in 25 treatment-refractory patients (median dose, 20 mg; range, 15–30 mg; mean age, 9.1 ± 5.7 years). In an open-label prospective study, 17 patients with severe VKC unresponsive to topical corticosteroids and dual-acting agents (mean age, 12.3 ± 3.65 years) received triamcinolone 20 mg; all had significant keratitis improvement, smaller giant papillae, and complete resolution of eyelid swelling and conjunctival chemosis. Reinjection was needed in 5 patients after a mean of 13.1 months; recurrences in the others were controllable topically. Effects of supratarsal corticosteroids on intraocular pressure remain uncertain: some studies and case series found no increase, whereas others reported increases in 6% to 17% of treated patients.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2.2. Calcineurin inhibitors.
document_sections.content: Cyclosporine A (CsA) and tacrolimus modulate VKC immunity by blocking IL-2-mediated proliferation of Th2 lymphocytes. Both have long been used off-label and have demonstrated good efficacy for moderate-to-severe VKC.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2.2.1. Cyclosporine.
document_sections.content: Cyclosporine A binds cyclophilin-1 inside T cells; the resulting complex prevents calcineurin-dependent transcription of IL-2 and other inflammatory cytokines and thereby inhibits T-cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation. Topical CsA improves corneal-surface integrity and protects conjunctival epithelial cells through an antiapoptotic effect. Systemic exposure after topical application is negligible, allowing local immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory effects without weakening general immunity or damaging ocular structures. Compounded cyclosporine drops have been used off-label in VKC since the late 1980s. Studies of differing formulations and concentrations report safety and efficacy, although ocular opportunistic infection risk, burning, and irritation remain concerns. In a prospective study of 156 children and adolescents receiving compounded cyclosporine (1% and 2%), follow-up lasted up to 7 years (mean, 3.8 years); objective ocular scores improved significantly over time, with significant improvement at the beginning and end of each seasonal treatment period with evaluable data. Earlier 2% preparations, often mixed with olive or castor oil, caused treatment-limiting transient burning and foreign-body sensation on instillation. CsA 0.05% preparations consistently outperformed placebo but sometimes did not fully treat or prevent flares. CSA 1.0% formulations showed good tolerability and efficacy for 4 months in a double-blind placebo-controlled study and for up to 7 years in a single-center prospective study. EAACI recommends CsA eye drops to reduce corticosteroid requirements in corticosteroid-dependent VKC. Evidence mainly concerns topical use, although at least 1 case report suggests oral CsA might spare corticosteroids: a 6-year-old child with severe refractory VKC of 4.5 years' duration had a marked response to 75–150 mg/day, including shield-ulcer resolution, permitting withdrawal of oral corticosteroids and use of a lower-potency topical corticosteroid. Topical ocular delivery is limited because up to 80% of a drug is estimated to drain nasolacrimally within 2 minutes; CsA's insolubility and lipophilicity also complicate exposure. CsA cationic ophthalmic emulsion (CsA CE) uses positively charged, oil-containing droplets dispersed in water to improve contact with the negatively charged ocular surface. Oily droplet cores dissolve CsA and surfactant coatings stabilize the emulsion; attraction to ocular cell membranes improves spreading and doubles corneal CsA concentration, enhancing bioavailability and effect. CsA CE 0.1% is approved for VKC in multiple Asian, European, and North American countries. Health Canada approved it in 2018 for severe VKC from 4 years of age through adolescence, at 1 drop per eye 4 times daily (q.i.d.); after adequate control, dosing may stay unchanged or decrease to 1 drop twice daily (b.i.d.). In June of 2021, the United States Food and Drug Administration approved CsA CE 0.1% q.i.d. (1 drop per eye) for children and adults with VKC. Approval relied on phase 3 VEKTIS (NCT01751126) and supportive phase II/lll NOVATIVE trials in patients 4–21 years of age. Multicenter, randomized, vehicle-controlled VEKTIS included a 4-month efficacy/safety phase and an 8-month double-masked extension. During the initial phase, 169 patients aged 4–17 years with severe VKC received CsA CE 0.1% q.i.d., CsA CE 0.1% b.i.d., or vehicle. The composite efficacy measure combined keratitis assessed with corneal fluorescein staining (CFS) using the modified Oxford scale, rescue-medication use, and corneal-ulcer occurrence; CFS was also a secondary endpoint. At 4 months, composite scores improved significantly against vehicle with q.i.d. (P = 0.007) and b.i.d. (P = 0.010). Change in CFS from baseline explained 70.3% of treatment effect with q.i.d. and 77.6% with b.i.d. Relative to vehicle, the q.i.d. group reported significant reductions in photophobia (P < 0.001), tearing (P < 0.009), itching (P = 0.001), and mucous discharge (P = 0.005), alongside better QoL (P < 0.05). Improvements in keratitis, symptoms, and QoL persisted through the 8-month extension. During the 4-month efficacy phase, 1 or more rescue courses of dexamethasone 0.1% q.i.d. for ≤5 days were required by 32.1% of the CsA CE 0.1% q.i.d. group versus 53.4% of the vehicle group (P = 0.010). Multicenter, randomized, double-masked, parallel-group NOVATIVE enrolled patients ≥4 years old with moderate-to-severe VKC (N = 118). Its first 4-week period allocated patients 1:1:1 to CsA CE 0.05% q.i.d., CsA CE 0.1% q.i.d., or vehicle; the second period provided CsA CE 0.05% or 0.1% q.i.d. for another 3 months. Pooled NOVATIVE and VEKTIS safety data identified instillation-site pain (high dose, 9.4%; low dose, 7.5%) and pruritis (high dose, 5.2%; low dose, 7.5%) as the most frequent reactions among CsA CE recipients. Most adverse events were mild-to-moderate, and systemic CsA absorption was negligible with both dose regimens.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2.2.2. Tacrolimus.
document_sections.content: Tacrolimus is a macrolide lactone obtained by fermenting Streptomyces tsukubaensis. It binds immunophilin FK-binding proteins, including FKBP-12, inhibits calcineurin, and interrupts nuclear factor of activated T-cells (NFAT) activation and IL-2 transcription. Although systemic tacrolimus has been a more effective immunosuppressant than CsA after organ transplantation, direct ocular comparisons remain limited. Topical treatment in VKC can cause burning upon installation and increase corneal-infection risk. Drops and ointment are widely used off-label; compounded concentrations from 0.003% to 1.0%, administered b.i.d. or q.i.d., have significantly improved VKC manifestations with negligible systemic absorption. Tacrolimus ointment is approved only as second-line treatment for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis; for children 2–15 years old, only 0.03% is indicated under that approval. Tacrolimus 0.1% ophthalmic suspension has been approved in Japan since 2008. As of September 2023, ClinicalTrials.gov listed 8 tacrolimus VKC trials. Available evidence largely comes from small case reports, case series, and open-label uncontrolled studies with varied formulations and regimens. Comparisons with compounded cyclosporine have produced mixed results; no direct comparison with CsA CE 0.1% had been conducted at the time of writing. A prospective double-masked randomized study of 24 patients with active VKC (mean age, 9.61 ± 2.55 years) compared tacrolimus 0.1% ointment b.i.d. with CsA 2% drops q.i.d.; both significantly improved subjective symptoms without significant between-group efficacy or safety differences, although instillation-related burning was slightly less bothersome with tacrolimus. A prospective randomized double-blind study in 32 children (mean age, 7.62 ± 1.82 years) similarly found significant total-symptom-score reductions with tacrolimus ointment 0.03% b.i.d. and cyclosporine 0.05% q.i.d., without significant between-group differences. By contrast, a prospective study of 59 children with refractory VKC reported significantly greater reductions in redness, burning, photophobia, foreign-body sensation, conjunctival papillary hypertrophy, and cobblestone papillae with tacrolimus 0.03% ointment than with CsA 2% drops. An Italian double-blind crossover study enrolled 30 children (mean age 9.05 ± 2.12 years) who had not responded to cyclosporine drops for at least 15 days. Compared with compounded cyclosporine 1.0% drops, tacrolimus 0.1% drops administered 3 times daily produced significantly greater improvement in subjective symptoms, disease severity, and QoL; adverse effects were generally mild and similar, and serum drug concentrations were negligible. A later retrospective study of 431 children refractory to conventional treatment, including CsA drops (1–2%), 1 drop per eye, 3 times a day, defined refractoriness as requiring topical or oral corticosteroids alongside topical CsA for better clinical control. Tacrolimus 0.1% drops significantly reduced papillae and conjunctival redness, with striking improvement within 3 months. Partly on this evidence, EAACI recommends reserving off-label tacrolimus drops or ointment for severe VKC refractory to CsA.

document_sections.heading: 6.3. Allergen-specific immunotherapy
document_sections.content: For patients with identified allergens, sublingual (SLIT) or subcutaneous (SCIT) allergen-specific immunotherapy gradually increases exposure to desensitize the patient and modify disease. Treatment takes months to years but can improve systemic manifestations and reduce topical or systemic medication needs. In a prospective comparison involving patients with VKC (N = 64; mean age approximately 13.5 years), SCIT improved symptoms and reduced serum IgE significantly more than topical therapy. After successful SLIT in a treatment-refractory 8-year-old boy, Bernales and colleagues proposed immunotherapy as a primary treatment when specific allergen reactions are known. Because approximately half of VKC patients lack allergic sensitization, its suitability is confined to a relatively small subgroup.

document_sections.heading: 6.4.1. Leukotriene inhibition
document_sections.content: Leukotrienes have long been considered possible VKC treatment targets. Oral montelukast inhibits leukotrienes and is approved for asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis. In an uncontrolled study of patients with asthma and VKC (N = 12), montelukast was associated with significant improvements in ocular findings and symptoms, including redness, tearing, and photophobia. A larger open-label randomized controlled pediatric VKC study (N = 58) found clinically and statistically significant improvements in redness, itching, foreign-body sensation, and tearing with montelukast versus mast cell stabilizers in moderate-to-severe disease.

document_sections.heading: 6.4.2. Interleukin antagonists
document_sections.content: Dupilumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that blocks IL-4, IL-13, and Th2-mediated inflammation through cytokine-secretion blockade; these pathways participate in conjunctival papilla formation in ocular allergy. Subcutaneous dupilumab is approved for severe refractory atopic dermatitis. Conjunctivitis and keratitis were more frequent among dupilumab recipients in clinical trials. A claims analysis of patients prescribed dupilumab (N = 2144) between January 1, 2016 and June 30, 2019 likewise found more ocular-surface-disorder healthcare encounters after treatment initiation. Conversely, case reports of patients with atopic dermatitis or asthma alongside severe AKC and VKC described improvements, including in giant papillae. A retrospective series of 3 patients with corticosteroid-refractory VKC reported significant relief of itching, photophobia, ocular discomfort, foreign-body sensation, and tearing with dupilumab. Shield ulcers resolved, conjunctival redness and eyelid swelling decreased, and upper tarsal giant papillae resolved completely in all patients. A multicenter double-masked randomized placebo-controlled parallel-group study (N = 42; NCT04296864) assessing dupilumab for atopic keratoconjunctivitis was recruiting. Rebamipide, derived from quinolone-class antibiotics, stimulates mucin secretion, lowers IL-6 and IL-8 production, reduces eosinophil infiltration, and inhibits TNF-α. It has significantly reduced papilla formation in conventionally treatment-refractory VKC and AKC; reported adverse effects include dysgeusia and eyelid itching. IL-5 is important for eosinophil activation, and targeting it has worked in eosinophil-mediated disease, particularly asthma. The asthma therapies benralizumab, mepolizumab, and reslizumab may be useful for VKC, but this potential is not presented as established VKC efficacy. Benralizumab binds IL-5Rα on eosinophils and basophils and lowers serum eosinophils; it is approved as intravenous adjunct treatment for severe eosinophilic asthma in children over the age of 12. Mepolizumab is an IL-5-directed IgG1-type antibody approved as add-on maintenance treatment for eosinophilic asthma in adults and children aged 6 years and older. Reslizumab is an IL-5-directed IgG4-type antibody with similar effects on eosinophils, approved as add-on maintenance treatment for severe eosinophilic asthma in patients aged 18 years and older.

document_sections.heading: 6.4.3. IgE blockade
document_sections.content: Omalizumab is a recombinant humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds free IgE, an initiator of allergic inflammation. It is approved for severe persistent asthma; off-label case reports suggest a possible role in treatment-refractory VKC. In a chart review of 4 boys with severe VKC, defined by persistent corneal inflammation despite continuous topical 2% cyclosporine and steroid drops, 3 of 4 had fewer symptoms, shorter flares, and reduced steroid requirements after omalizumab. Reports of monthly or biweekly subcutaneous doses from 225 to 600 mg describe improved erythema and cobblestone papillae, reduced burning and/or itching, and less need for topical antihistamines within 2 months of starting treatment. Regimens and responses varied, potentially because of non-IgE disease mechanisms; one child whose treatment failed had no allergic sensitization. In contrast, a patient with atopic dermatitis, refractory VKC, and extremely high serum IgE had broad improvement in skin and ocular symptoms within 4 weeks of the first subcutaneous omalizumab 300 mg dose.

document_sections.heading: 6.4.4. Other targets
document_sections.content: Sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectin (Siglec)-8 is an inhibitory receptor on mast cells, eosinophils, and basophils. Antibody engagement can suppress mast cell activation and induce apoptosis of activated eosinophils. Preclinical findings indicate that the Siglec-8-directed antibody lirentelimab (AK002) kills eosinophils and inhibits mast cell activation. In a phase 1b study involving 30 patients with severe allergic conjunctivitis, including one with VKC, 6 months of AK002 treatment was associated with an 87% improvement in allergic conjunctivitis score for the patient with VKC.

document_sections.heading: 7. Comparative data and treatment selection
document_sections.content: Increasing treatment options complicate selection. Differences among studies in designs, populations, outcomes, formulations, and dosing hinder conclusions applicable to routine care. Meta-analyses of topical therapy generally report no significant efficacy differences among frequently used agents. A 2007 meta-analysis of 27 double-masked VKC trials involving 1092 patients found reductions in clinical signs and symptoms with every evaluated drug; more than 70% of included studies compared mast cell stabilizers with other treatments. A review by Roumeau and colleagues examined 45 articles covering 1749 patients treated with 20 drugs. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus were most often studied, followed by mast cell inhibitors; all evaluated therapies improved manifestations, with no significant differences between specific drugs. VKC heterogeneity makes a universal treatment algorithm difficult. Despite regional and national guidance, individual plans must account for symptom periodicity and severity, corneal involvement, and patient needs and goals. Broadly shared principles include symptom control with minimal adverse effects, individualization according to severity and pathology, patient education, and nonpharmacologic care. A group of 7 European ophthalmologists used a modified nominal group technique to formulate 47 VKC-management recommendations, emphasizing prompt diagnosis and severity-aligned treatment to prevent visual loss and improve children's QoL. The Management of Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis in Asia Expert Working Group likewise advocates stepped care incorporating trigger identification, education about ocular health, and treatments for VKC symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 8. Future directions
document_sections.content: Much VKC research comprises small nonrandomized studies that may be unable to identify meaningful treatment-group differences. Adequately powered comparisons of treatment efficacy and safety are needed to strengthen evidence for diagnostic criteria and treatment guidelines. Such guidance could aid differential diagnosis and treatment selection as therapies with varied mechanisms become available. Research should establish optimal therapy sequencing or combinations, including possible synergy between immunotherapy and topical drugs. Differences in responses across individual manifestations expose the limitations of composite efficacy scores. Separate reporting of each sign and symptom, supported by consensus on core VKC outcomes, could enable more individualized treatment. Greater attention to QoL and use of validated measures such as QUICK in trials and care plans could improve understanding of patient burden and communication among clinicians, patients, and caregivers, supporting treatment adherence.

document_sections.heading: 9. Conclusions
document_sections.content: VKC is a chronic ocular-surface disorder that can be seasonal or perennial and can endanger vision. Its prevalence differs widely by region, and overlap with other allergic conjunctivitides can delay or misdirect diagnosis, especially where VKC is rare. Because disease progresses, such delays can seriously impair functioning and QoL. Rather than being solely IgE-mediated, VKC involves multiple immune processes, including increased mast cells, Th2 cells, eosinophils, and inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules. Treatment previously depended mainly on topical mast cell stabilizers, corticosteroids, and off-label agents for symptom relief or immune modulation. Approval of CsA CE 0.1% offers an important corticosteroid-sparing alternative; further topical and systemic options, including monoclonal antibodies against inflammatory pathways, may follow. Allergen avoidance, behavioral changes, and adherence to complex topical or systemic regimens often need to be combined. Clinicians should recognize the burden on children and caregivers, individualize treatment, explain VKC and its therapeutic options, and help patients adhere to their plans.

document_sections.heading: 10. Method of literature search
document_sections.content: The authors searched PubMed Medline for English-language literature from 2016 through 2022 using (“vernal keratoconjunctivitis” OR VKC) AND (diagnosis OR treatment OR prevalence OR presentation OR signs OR symptoms OR incidence OR pathogenesis). They reviewed and included relevant articles, prioritizing prospective studies and randomized clinical trials. Relevant retrospective studies, case reports, reviews, and meta-analyses were also eligible. Reference lists of selected publications were examined for additional relevant work absent from the electronic search.
